title: How to Troubleshoot an HVAC System
h1: How Do I Troubleshoot My HVAC System Before Calling for Repair?
description: A step-by-step HVAC troubleshooting guide for homeowners: thermostat, filter, breakers, drain line and outdoor unit checks, and when it is time to call a pro.
quick_answer: Start with the simple checks: thermostat settings and batteries, the air filter, the breakers and the furnace service switch, the condensate drain safety switch, and a clear outdoor unit. Those fix a surprising number of problems. If the system still won't run, blows warm air, freezes up or trips breakers, it's time for a technician.
body:
Is the thermostat set correctly?

It sounds obvious, but the thermostat causes a lot of service calls. Check these first:

  • The mode is set to Heat or Cool, not Off or Fan only
  • The setpoint is a few degrees above room temperature for heat or below it for cooling
  • The screen isn't blank. If it is, replace the batteries.
  • Smart thermostats aren't in an eco, away or vacation mode, and the schedule is correct
  • The thermostat isn't in direct sun or near a lamp, which throws off its reading

Is the air filter clogged?

A dirty filter is behind many problems that look serious. It can cause weak airflow, a frozen AC coil, a furnace that overheats and shuts off, and higher bills. Pull the filter out and look at it. If it's gray and you can't see light through it, replace it.

If the AC coil froze because of a dirty filter, turn the system to Off and the fan to On for a few hours to let it thaw before running cooling again.

Is the system getting power?

If nothing happens at all when you change the thermostat:

  1. Check the breakers for the furnace or air handler and the outdoor unit at the main panel. A tripped breaker sits in the middle or off position.
  2. Check the service switch near the furnace or air handler. It looks like a light switch and is easy to flip off by accident, especially in a garage or hall closet.
  3. Check the outdoor disconnect beside the AC or heat pump.
  4. Make sure the furnace door is closed tightly, since a safety switch cuts power when it's loose.

Reset a tripped breaker once. If it trips again, leave it off and call for service.

Is water shutting the system down?

Air conditioners and high-efficiency furnaces produce water that drains away through a condensate line. Many systems have a float switch that shuts everything off when the drain backs up. Look for water in the drain pan under the indoor unit or a small switch on the drain line.

A clogged drain is common in homes with attic units, where a backup can also leak into ceilings. If you see water, turn the system off and have the drain cleared.

What should I check on the outdoor unit?

With the system calling for cooling, go outside and look and listen:

  • Is the fan on top spinning?
  • Do you hear the compressor running, a steady hum underneath the fan noise?
  • Is the coil clear of leaves, dirt, cobwebs and plants?
  • Is there ice on the copper lines?

Trim plants back about two feet and gently rinse a dirty coil with a garden hose, never a pressure washer. If the fan isn't spinning, you hear a loud buzz or clicking, or there's ice, turn the system off. Those usually point to a failed capacitor, motor or refrigerant problem that needs a technician.

Common symptoms and what they usually mean

SymptomCommon causes
Blowing warm air in cooling modeOutdoor unit off, dirty coil, low refrigerant, failed capacitor
Weak airflowDirty filter, frozen coil, leaky or crushed ducts
Short cyclingDirty filter, oversized system, thermostat location, overheating furnace
Furnace starts then shuts offDirty flame sensor, clogged filter, venting problem
Some rooms too hot or coldDuct leaks, closed vents, poor insulation

When should I stop troubleshooting and call a pro?

Homeowners can safely handle the thermostat, filter, breakers, drain pan and keeping the outdoor unit clear. Leave refrigerant, electrical components, gas valves and burners to a technician. Call for help when:

  • A breaker trips more than once
  • You hear grinding, banging or screeching
  • You smell burning or see scorched wiring
  • The system runs but can't keep up on a normal day

If you smell gas, leave the house and call the gas utility from outside. If a carbon monoxide alarm sounds, get out and call 911. For everything else, our HVAC repair team can diagnose the problem, and you can reach us here to set up a visit.
faqs: Why is my AC running but not cooling?

Common reasons are a dirty filter, a frozen coil, a dirty outdoor coil, the outdoor unit not running because of a tripped breaker or failed capacitor, or low refrigerant. Check the filter and outdoor unit first, then call for service.
Why does my furnace turn on and then shut off?
Often it's a dirty flame sensor, a clogged filter causing overheating, or a venting problem. The furnace shuts down as a safety measure. A technician can clean the sensor and check the rest.
Can I add refrigerant to my AC myself?
No. Handling refrigerant requires certification and the right equipment. Low refrigerant also means there's a leak, which should be found and repaired rather than just topped off.
How often should my HVAC system be serviced?
Once a year for each system is a good rule. Many homeowners schedule AC service in spring before the hot months and furnace service in fall before cold nights.
